source.title: Stochastic Monkeys at Play: Random Augmentations Cheaply Break LLM Safety Alignment
source.authors: Jason Vega; Junsheng Huang; Gaokai Zhang; Hangoo Kang; Minjia Zhang; Gagandeep Singh

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests harmful-request compliance under random prompt augmentations and decoding changes, using a different intervention from fine-tuning or measuring per-token KL.
record.gate_note: The paper measures judge-assessed harmful-request success under random prompt augmentations and temperature sampling. It does not test fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples, per-token KL, compliant response prefilling, or safety localization in parameters. Its in-text experiment prompts and examples are not reviewer-directed instructions.
record.test_reason: The study reports judge-rated harmful compliance of safety-aligned chat models under random suffixes and higher sampling temperature (Table 7). These are the suffix and decoding routes V4 names, although the suffixes are random rather than optimized. It does not fine-tune, measure per-token KL, prefill, localize weights or deepen alignment.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that cheap random augmentations with 25 attempts raise harmful success by up to about 11-21% for aligned models under greedy decoding, with character-level changes beating string insertion. Temperature alone raises success; adding augmentations on top of sampling generally hurts, but deletion still helps for Llama 2, Llama 3 and Phi 3. They also report that larger models tend to be safer, aggressive quantization less safe, and that fine-tuning defenses help but R2D2 over-refuses suffixed benign prompts.
record.recipe_differences: Uses random character-level and string-insertion prompt augmentations, plus temperature sampling; it does not fine-tune models or measure response-position KL. The evaluated suffixes are random, not optimized adversarial suffixes.
record.method_sensitivity: Augmentation type matters: character-level changes generally outperform string insertion. Sampling temperature changes baseline success and often reduces the additional gain from random augmentation. Model, system prompt, and augmentation strength also vary in experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Random character-level edits and deletions inside the prompt raise harmful success more than random suffixes do (e.g. Llama 3 edit +0.253 vs suffix +0.024). Under sampling, their added effect shrinks or vanishes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety refusal is brittle to small tokenization-altering perturbations of the harmful request itself.

record.problems: The main safety measure uses a learned judge. The authors calibrate its threshold with human judgments on a sample of 1220 data points, but report no uncertainty intervals for the tabulated outcomes. Evaluation uses 450 SORRY-Bench prompts. The authors note that judge-assessed success does not always correspond to equally harmful response content.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, omitted separate Prefix and Anywhere string-insertion results and character-level Insert results from Table 7; omitted τ=0.7 no-augmentation rate rows, the system-prompt results in Table 4, GPT-4o results in Table 3, augmentation-strength ablations in Figures 9–10, and fixed-length suffix/defense outcomes in Figure 6 and Table 11. These are outside the retained subset or duplicate the included conditions; Table 7 reports the omitted augmentation types and τ=0.7 rates.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant response start; optimized adversarial suffixes such as GCG; decoding changes other than two temperature values (no top-p/top-k search); any link to first-token shallowness.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
Weight or rank localization of safety. Quantization is tested, but not as localization.
Training that deepens safety. RR and R2D2 defenses are evaluated, but not safety depth.

missing.what: Random suffix gains under temperature sampling: negative for all aligned models (e.g. Llama 3 -0.087 at τ=0.7, -0.116 at τ=1.0). Not declared in rows_left_out, and bears on combining the suffix and decoding routes.
Random prefix-string insertion gains, greedy and sampled (e.g. Llama 3 -0.002 greedy). Declared as left out, but they qualify the suffix result.

record.verdict_notes: This is not an original source. The reader linked character-level augmentations and unaligned models to V4; I unlinked them because V4 names suffixes, prefills and decoding changes on safety-trained models. Several small negative D-row gains are re-stated as absent. Success is judged by a learned judge with a calibrated threshold, and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples and whether it removes refusals.
Fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully selected benign data.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models, including its distribution across response positions.

No compliant assistant-opening prefilling or optimized adversarial suffix is tested. The paper tests random suffix insertion, other random character augmentations, and temperature sampling; it does not test other decoding changes.
Weight or rank localization of safety behaviour.
Whether training data or objective causes first-token shallowness.

Training explicitly designed to spread safety beyond the first tokens and measuring that distribution. The paper evaluates existing fine-tuning-based defenses against random augmentations, but not safety depth.

relationships.condition: Random (non-optimized) suffix, greedy decoding, safety-aligned Llama 2/3/3.1, Phi 3 Small, Qwen 2 7B, k=25
relationships.reason: Suffix gains are only +0.024 to +0.100 over no augmentation, far from defeating refusal (G-L2-S, G-L3-S, G-L31-S, G-P3-S, G-Q2-S). From Table 7 text, suffix gains turn negative under sampling.
relationships.display_finding: Under greedy decoding, random suffixes added only +0.024 to +0.100 over no augmentation. Under sampling the gains turned negative.
